transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for metamodern mutants interested in meditation, awakening, Vajrayana, Tantra, Zen, Pirates of the Caribbean, psychedelics, non-duality, consciousness hacking, and much, much more. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode I'm speaking with Wystan. Wystan is a meditation teacher, threading together influences from Theravada, Zen, Vajrayana, Dzogchen, and Shinzen Young's systematic secular approach in service of awakening. And now, without further ado, I give you a conversation with Wystan.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Wystan, welcome to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Thank you for welcoming me. Long-time listener, first-time caller. Delighted to be here, Michael. Thank you so much for inviting me on.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, I'm super delighted to have you on the podcast. And I've been on your show, so nice to bring you on here. Where in the world are you located right now, Wystan? I know you're traveling around.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Yeah, well, I got divorced last year, Michael. And since, I've been relying on the generosity of friends and family and have spent a little more than five months in retreat, either teaching or participating. So I've been bouncing all around. But right now I'm at my parents' place on the island of Crete in Greece. My dad's an Anglican minister with the Church of England, and he's ministering to expatriate Brits who are here for the low cost of living. So that's where I'm hanging out for the next couple of weeks, and then off again.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Is Crete a fun place to hang out?

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: It is. I mean, as you can imagine, Mediterranean island, beautiful. It's just unreasonably gorgeous.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. Now, in our pre-talk you said you just got out of a retreat. What kind of retreat were you doing?

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Yeah. So I was in retreat with Mugen Roshi slash Stephen Snyder. When I started meeting with him and working with him, he was just Stephen. He didn't have the Zen transmission and title. Yeah. We were doing jhana, and his, the lineage of that, which he carries through Pa Auk Sayadaw.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, he's a Pa Auk Sayadaw guy. So those are hardcore, super deep jhanas. How's that going?

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Yeah, the nut jhanas. Man, it's a delight. If you, like me, are a bum and like deep meditation, just doing nothing but attending one-pointedly to the breath for 14 to 20 hours a day and getting into ludicrously non-concentrated, non-dual states. Yeah, it's the best thing going.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That sounds amazing. Okay. Well, let's see what's on your mind today. I brought you on to talk about whatever you'd like to talk about. So what is it that you would like to talk about?

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Which was a difficult question in our pre-conversation, because I've had a lot on my mind. One of the things, though, is that a mutual friend of ours is opening this spiritual but non-religious center in Boulder, Colorado. And as I've stepped into a teaching position and—

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: But they haven't figured out a name yet.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: No, they've got— oh, well. Yes. But over the last couple of years, as I've stepped into a teaching role and I've seen other people move through phases of their teaching career in and outside of kind of traditional lineage contexts, but especially in the kind of para-lineage position that I'm in and you're in, I think I can be fair to say, where there is engagement with traditional lineage, there may be deep experience there, but for whatever reason there isn't the traditional kind of career track, if you like, within a particular lineage leading to then teaching. In my case, that's partly because most of the training I've done is in cloistered monastic contexts. And for a while I was intent on shaving my head, going forth from the home life into the homeless life. That ceased to make sense after a while, and I felt a definitive call and a pull back out into the world, and yet still have done, you know, and continue to go back. I was in a monastery for three months this past winter. But ordained life, not for me. And yet some of my teachers have encouraged me to go out to teach, and I did training with Shinzen Young. So it can be difficult in a way that's fully authentic to one's more traditional training, while not claiming to represent a specific kind of stream. You're not offering exactly what the lineage is offering. But it's also— one of my teachers has advised me it's good to acknowledge one's influences, and also not claim to represent that particular brand, to maintain the integrity and the distinction.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's right. I mean, this is the idea, at least the way I understand it and the way I try to play it or do it, is we acknowledge our teachers, we acknowledge our sources, and at the same time, for example, I'm always careful to say, yeah, this is maybe coming from Mahamudra or coming from Dzogchen. And I'll almost always add, and I am not an ordained Mahamudra or Dzogchen teacher. I don't do it every time, but I do it often enough, because it's important to make that distinction.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Yeah. But even being careful, you can't please everybody. And I don't know how often you experience this, but Buddhists— being one myself and having some of these tendencies myself, we get very persnickety drawing the boundaries and policing what is kosher and what is not. I think the Buddha might've had something to say about that, clinging to views. There's something in there.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, yeah. So lay out your position here, since you're bringing up— this is interesting. Let's go here.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Well, my position is that awakening, the freedom the Buddha realized and taught, attempted to teach for all his life, it doesn't come with a Buddhist label. And at least in my consideration of my activity in the world, what is good for me to bring forth, what I've been encouraged to by some of my teachers to bring forth— I reckon that with my cultural conditioning background, the societal context, I was not actually going to be most effective in offering that to people and being of use within the confines of a monastic role, title, career track, and being more open, available, and accessible to people and communicating with them in language that made sense to them. Sometimes that is fully traditional language. We can talk about the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Noble Path. We can go there.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, of course. But I do agree strongly, actually, that for most people, most of the time, that's probably not the most effective presentation, and that there's a whole other way of talking about this type of material, teaching, awakening type material, that our culture is still trying to come up with. What I think is interesting is that, of course, Buddhism has always been an export religion, right? They've always had missionaries, they're always moving to new cultures and new countries. And so it is completely historically the case that each new culture, each new country has to kind of reinvent it from scratch to make it their own. In other words, to make it work in their cultural context. Now, of course, this is best done with guidance from people who know what they're talking about in the previous culture or teaching context, obviously, right? We don't just run off willy-nilly and teach anything.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: I mean, some people do.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Some people do. You're right. But that might not work that well. Let's just put it that way. But on the other hand, trying to use these forms that were invented 1,000 or 2,000 years ago in a completely different cultural context, in a completely different language, and that have often already been translated like 10 times from different languages, et cetera, et cetera— it's traditional. Ironically, it's traditional to have to kind of remake this for one's own culture, and that often takes several hundred years, at least historically.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Yeah, yeah. So we're very much culturally, and within my own engagement with the Dharma just in the span of my own life, things have changed a lot. We're in a process of real gestation. And being a relative newcomer to teaching and, all things considered, discounting the possibility that I may have been engaged on this path for innumerable past lifetimes, even within the course of my own life, you know, it hasn't been too terribly long— all my adult life, but life is long, one hopes. One hopes. Could die tomorrow. Always a possibility. It feels very early in the culture and in my own teachers' lives and presentations. And I've been fortunate to have a bunch of great teachers. And in my own fumbling expression, starting now, only a couple of years into teaching, you see people swerve this way and that. Some of my teachers are very conservative. I was at Meido Roshi's monastery in Wisconsin, Korinji, for three months this winter, and it's like living in medieval Japan. And that's fantastic. It works exceptionally well. And then there are folks like Shinzen who are taking a huge range of all of their influences and really working it over decades into something that doesn't look particularly Buddhist in language anyway at all. And I guess what I'm trying to figure out, maybe you can help me out, Michael, is— what I care about is awakening and helping people do that as is appropriate for them.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, this is certainly my passion and what I'm trying to do with my life, right? Is to give that gift to folks, or whatever language you want to— Buddha, help people to find that for themselves. Maybe it's a better way to say it. And it's interesting because, again, we're from such a different culture, it doesn't often necessarily look all that Buddhist in terms of its upfront language and all that, even if the essence of Buddhism is awakening. And so as long as it's teaching awakening, I would say it is getting to the core of Buddhism. It's in the name, after all. Buddha, what does that mean?

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: All right. Exactly. Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: This is about awakeness. And so that's kind of the most broad possible definition. And you see in the course of Shinzen's teaching— I've known him since the mid-90s and got to work with him one-on-one, not only in meditation stuff, but also to help him create his books and audio programs and stuff for many, many years.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And something that's been really fascinating is to watch the teaching change and grow and change and grow and become ever more idiosyncratic. And he's iterating on what he finds works, what people respond to, the language they understand. And I think that's something that really attracted me to him initially. I was in a very, very, let's say, very traditional Hindu Tantra lineage that was as old school as it's possible to get. So running into someone who was like, let's talk about languages, let's talk about cultures, let's talk about all these different ways that this has expressed over time, let's talk about different religions, let's bring in the science— and willing to just talk about it all in a very open and quite modern manner, this is way back in the 90s, was incredibly exciting and interesting and powerful and drew me right in, right? It's like, let's look at all this stuff from a new lens.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And so it's been super fascinating to watch how that's been growing and changing and growing and changing over time. But I think the main point is just that when we start working in that direction, iterating on what seems to work for people, especially in our culture, that might start to go off in a pretty unusual direction. But on the other hand, Shinzen is obviously steeped in very traditional Buddhist practice, especially Zen, but other lineages as well. Plus there's a ton of awakening there. So lo and behold, it tends to work even if it sounds pretty different. And this is the interesting thing. I think we might be at the place societally where we're kind of rocketing towards maximum difference. Like all the teachers are teaching— not all of them, but many, many, many teachers are teaching in all these various different idiosyncratic sounding ways. And we're kind of exploring the space, exploring the space, exploring the space to see what actually works. And so I wonder if one of these days, one of these decades, we're going to start coming together again about how this really lands for people in this time, this day and age, this culture and so on.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Let a thousand flowers bloom, a thousand lotuses. And maybe there'll be something more coherent at the other end that is more adapted. I mean, I notice a trend in myself even. I kind of oscillate between these two poles sometimes, feeling the rapid change, the ground shifting underneath economically, socially, geopolitically. And there's a tendency then to cling to the old, to the sure, to what is proven over thousands of years. Well, this language, these forms, this presentation, it definitely works. So better hold fast, even as the world changes, it seems, ever more rapidly around us. And then at the same time, that also opens up room for experimentation and play. There's opportunity and aliveness.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. And that brings up my question, which is, but does it work in the translated way that we're experiencing it, and in translated forms that we're trying to adapt from another culture, et cetera, et cetera, right? I mean, of course, no one's questioning— of course it works in the, where it's coming from, but how well does it work here, for how many people? Freaks like even me, who love alternative culture stuff, just dive in and it's like, okay, make me a medieval Hindu peasant or whatever, the medieval Indian peasant or Japanese whatever, I'm game, just go there. But that's very rare, actually.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Yeah, I don't know if you found this, Michael, but when attempting to teach other folks and pass something useful along, I find again and again, other people aren't me. I can't just be like, hey, this is what worked for me, just do it. I don't know, it doesn't seem to land.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, or you can, and then that's a teeny tiny— then you're useless as a teacher, right? So yeah, it's fascinating.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: I think that there's an interesting— this might be a way in, a wedge, because I did teacher training, you know, with Shinzen, and that, the program that he set up, and that was very helpful. After looking at Shinzen doing a lot of that, helping me a lot with that kind of cultural translation as I was engaging, you know, in monasteries and out, engaging more traditional teachers and lineages, Theravada, Zen, Vajrayana— his kind of translational work was very, very helpful in me, and integrating, and then going through the teacher training and helping folks through that avenue. But I find personally, and for what I would like to present and move forward, a little bit of a pullback as well. Like the imagery, the language, the tradition, I feel, has more of a hold and a claim on me. And it's also, it's partly what I would like to pass on, you know, for those who do find the figure of the Buddha, who do find some of the traditional forms and language very resonant. There's a way in which I feel called, pulled to carry that a bit more than moving into a fully secular vocabulary without reference to the sources or the original Asian cultural context.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, tell me more. Dive in.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: In my own practice, so much of the fuel, the fire that has kept pulling me back in and deeper and deeper in, the original inspiration, was, I would say, really devotional. Coming from a place of deep, deep, deep suffering, but finding solace in these ancient texts that, you know, explained the nature of my predicament to me in a way that made sense and provided a path outward. The kind of the vocabulary, the language, the framing made sense, and also the figure of the Buddha, the early Sangha, people since who have followed the path and brought it to its culmination in this life, in this body— the richness of tradition. I think this is also probably informed by growing up in Christianity and having in my father an example of someone who really draws on and lives in the Umwelt of a faith tradition, you know, that was relatively familiar to me, knowing that that was kind of possible, to be so richly informed by tradition. And yet also there are just so many ways, especially trying to relate to others, where it's just like, I am not and cannot be a North Indian follower of the Buddha 2,500 years ago, or a medieval Tibetan Dzogchenpa, or a medieval Japanese Zen person. I've been incredibly fortunate to encounter these different streams of Dharma, but how that integrates and then expresses, you know, through this flimsy body and psychology, attempting to help others— work in progress, work in progress.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: You know, you used the word devotion, and this is like a forbidden word in the secular awakening community. And it's something that I'm grappling with a lot as a teacher, and I think it's super rich and interesting and fun kind of grappling. I mean, I like it. But the thing is that for me, I think that devotion is crucial. One must have devotion. And I would go so far as to say every single human being is wired for devotion. We are built that way, and every single human being is devoted to something or some things. But in our culture, devotion is either kind of poisonous for so many people— or, you know, I mean, traditional devotional forms end up being toxic for people— or they just throw the word out altogether and then have some kind of totally unconscious relationship to devotion. They end up being devoted to Ubuntu Linux or something, and that's their Jesus. And so, especially when we try to step out of traditional forms, I think it's really interesting to try to teach devotion while at the same time not telling people what to be devoted to, allowing them the freedom, within working with me anyway, to be devoted to whatever they want. You want to be devoted to the Buddha, great. You want to be devoted to universal awakening, great, whatever. Find your devotion.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: But that's obviously very non-traditional. And also it's really complicated, because you've got all these different people with all these different devotions. And yet in another way, it really lands, and it's really powerful when people start to realize what's there in devotion, and how important and rich and deep and human and mysterious and wonderful that kind of thing can be. And yet watching a whole group kind of trying to grapple with that and fumble towards it for themselves, to me, this is totally worth doing and completely fascinating. But it's also pretty different than saying, there's the Buddha, there's your devotion.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Yeah. Yeah. And I guess what struck me as a young man suffering so, seeing at first in an image, and then in glimpses, and then, you know, more deeply as practice went on, seeing in the image of the Buddha and practitioners and teachers I met— here is a dignified, lived expression of something fundamental, fundamental to being alive, to being a sentient being. Something that is clarified and awake and dignified, living in this conditioned world and knowing what is not born, what does not die, and living that, letting that clarify the life. That is something I could recognize in the texts that I read, and then getting actually acquainted with the practice, devoted to Buddha not as an image on an altar, not as a teacher that one, you know, relates to, but as something that is our nature, actually, already.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Right, that's the thing. And as soon as you make it that open, suddenly it's really open, right? So how do you deal with this when you're teaching?

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Oh gosh, very inexpertly, I'm quite sure. When I can tell that someone is caught up or hung up on a concept or on a framework, I'll try to get people to see that they're doing that and then let it go as swiftly as possible. Not that it isn't helpful to have some kind of orientation or map or direction, but the actual practice and the actual realization, it's just not that kind of thing. It isn't anything at all. Although it might be much more like the moment where you let that go. See how you're holding this delicate framework, and you've read this in a book and you've internalized it, and now you're representing it and you're bringing it out in speech, and there's a lot of contraction, massaging and fussing with all of that. If you can follow that letting go just all the way out, where does that leave you?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly. So interesting.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: There's always the opportunity to point directly to the awakeness that is already here for everyone at all times. If you're awake, if you're aware, it's there. It's always there.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And that's the thing. It's always there, even in all these modern forms or whatever.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Regardless of the confusion or the haggling and the debate and dispute over the forms, it is what underlies and gives rise, actually, to all of that. It's the context in which all of that occurs.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's right. And something that's so fascinating is that is the skeleton key that unlocks all these other traditions and languages and cultures and forms, right? You can read an interaction from the Blue Cliff Record or something and really get it, or taste it, or whatever, vibe with it, because the thread of awakening is there. You can hear it regardless of the time distance and cultural distance and language difference.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Recently, I was looking at this beautiful book called Luminous Melodies: Essential Dohas of Indian Mahamudra. It's translated by Karl Brunnholzl. And so you know what this is. This is Mahamudra's spontaneous songs of awakening. And they're wonderful and so beautiful. And you can just feel the light shining through them, even across all the centuries, even across all the cultures. It's just fabulous to dip into this and feel what they're experiencing. So the awakening is there, especially in that era of Mahamudra tradition. It's like, these are wild asses, just like crazy wisdom nutballs who are just singing about whatever they sing about. It doesn't often sound very Buddhist, but it's just amazing.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: No, awakening doesn't come with a label, nor does it care much for strict forms if they're getting in the way, right?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Without the label, without the strict forms. But it does come with a scent, and— or whatever, let's say a scent. And when you read something like this, it's like, there's the scent, whoa. And it just, it's just direct, even across the time, across space, it's just so beautiful. Here's a song by Nairatmya— Selflessness Embodied, that's the person's name, Nairatmya, Selflessness Embodied. “Space, space, great equality. The sun, the sun, great primordial lucidity. Rivers, rivers, the uninterrupted flow. Rainbows, great bliss free in itself.” Now realize that, everyone listening, in whatever is in front of you, in whatever sounds are arising, in whatever tactile sensations are present, in the liveliness of everything that appears. Just that. Just that. So point something out for us, Wystan.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: What's occurring right now, whatever sight, whatever sound, whatever sensation, eyes open or closed, the space within which all of this occurs, and the dance of that space, is already what everyone wants most deeply. The contact, the intimacy, the clarity, the vibrance is your own mind, always. And the dazzling clarity and wakefulness that you can't reach for, but you fall into, until there's no one falling. And then you're home.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Beautiful. Yeah, thanks for sharing that, from the heart. Where would you like to go from here, if anywhere?

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: All of the dispute and wrangling and controversy over the simplest thing there is, that's not even a thing. And power and wealth and influence over the millennia that has accrued over top and obscured the transmission from human person to human person, from body to body, from mind to mind. So that's the institutional religious layer, the frustration with that in the past and as it occurs now, and just how wasteful it all is. Then there's also tremendous heartbreak with everything occurring in the world, and have since I was very young, having early religious experiences, knowing it doesn't have to be this way. There's just blindness, and I'm prey to it. I'm blind. We're all blind, fumbling, not seeing clearly, not seeing clearly, not focusing on what's important. And we fight, we kill, we lash out verbally, all because we can't see what is closer to us than our own face. And it's heartbreaking. It's heartbreaking every day.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. I find that as the years and decades of practice go on and the practice does what it does, that it actually increases the heartbreak more and more. And when people say, man, my heart is breaking, and you can sometimes hear, just like I have heard in myself, but I can sometimes hear, they kind of wish that would stop. But at this point I'm like, no, that's compassion, right? That's heartbreak for the world, and that's breaking down barriers, and it's breaking down isolation and breaking down separateness. And when those start to fall, the feeling of just the intense sorrow for the whole of creation is very— poignant is a weak word in that case, but let's just say poignant.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Yeah. Your heart breaks open wider and wider until no thing and no one is left out. And it's hard to live up to that, but we try.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. And even being myself terrible at living up to it, still the experience is there. And it's something that after a while, I don't know what the word is, but you just start to get it, that that's the right direction. But to pull back for a minute, I agree. Right now, I mean, my God, it's just unbelievably heartbreaking how callous and blind and hyper devastating the world can be at times.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: But listening, listening to the heart, feeling what's occurring, not attempting to shunt or avoid. I mean, I don't know about you, but I've spent goodness knows countless hours diverting from the same heartbreak that turned me towards devotion, that turned me towards awakening. It's that same, that same impulse of compassion, of knowing that it doesn't have to be this way, and that there's something that I'm not seeing, that there's something that people aren't seeing. Turning into that is where the freedom is, not turning away.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's right. It's the only direction. And yet I still turn away. It's super pleasant to get involved in a movie or something like, wow, let's just not go there right now.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Even knowing that it's the right direction, the urge to turn away, it can still be so hard to resist.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's why I don't want to point fingers at anybody else, because it's quite seductive. And of course we live in a time and place where that particular form of seduction is— that's our real craft, right, of our society. We've learned to do that extremely well. I don't know what the percentage of our GDP is for any given country, that's wrapped up in keeping us pulled away from looking at the only thing that matters, but it's a lot. It's a lot. It's probably one of our main exports. And yet again, this is one of the things that the traditions are very good at reminding us: no, you got to turn into it, you got to turn into it, and open up and let it hurt.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: I think the Buddha might have had something to say about this, the first noble truth. I think there's something there.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Square one. Well, even as a somewhat non-traditionalist, although I am constantly teaching the traditions, but I do find it interesting how often I end up saying, yes, that's called dukkha. Like, there it is. That's what you're describing. That's the first noble truth. It's super fascinating.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: So what do we do? What do we do, Michael?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, you're the guest. You tell me. You're out there teaching retreats and stuff. So what do we do?

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: I can help people. I can help people wake up. I can do that.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: But it's a good thing to do.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Gotta do something.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's a good thing to do. That's right. I'll come back to a couple things. One is just keep your heart open as best you can, even if it's slammed shut a hundred times in a row and you make mistakes and you do bad things and all of that. We're humans, right? We still come back to trying to open up our heart every single day, again and again and again. And this is where I actually— I've never been very involved in 12-step, although I did start teaching meditation to 12-steppers before Shinzen said, yeah, you're qualified to teach. It's something I really like from 12-step, is like— and this comes back to the devotion conversation— but recognize that you might need some help. You might need some help. So not only open the heart, but come back to, basically, to not put too fine a point on it, praying for help.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: Yeah. And allowing devotion to not only crack you open further, but help you to open further. It's made for that. Devotion, heart practice, as I've gone along— I mean, where the juice is, where the further opening and the further clearly seeing what I have left to drop off, it's always along the dimension of opening the heart that allows me to see more clearly. Unless someone has a strong preference, it's where I'll start people off, is with the Brahma Viharas: loving kindness, sympathetic joy, compassion, equanimity.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, in my recent conversation with Stephen Snyder, he brought up two further Brahma Viharas, which I agree with him, at least one of them for sure. I think gratitude should be a neo-Brahma Vihara. If we're going to keep it in the same language, nava Brahma Vihara. And also forgiveness. Although I think forgiveness is a little different. Gratitude practice fits right in, I think, as a Brahma Vihara, and forgiveness practice, it just lands very different. It's a lot more complex than a Brahma Vihara. How do you feel?

transcript.speaker: Wystan
transcript.text: As a point of potential interest, I don't know, two thirds of the way through the recent retreat I was on with Mugen, with Stephen, where we are all very, very concentrated, certainly, he had us do forgiveness practice, and there wasn't a dry eye in the room.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, it's super powerful. Power of concentration, getting the system open, flowing, and then bringing in some forgiveness. For anyone listening, if you haven't tried that, worth doing.

transcript.speaker: Wystan
